It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. West Yorkshire Police has moved to reassure the public after a video appearing to show a man exposing himself at a bus stop in Leeds began circulating on social media again. The force confirmed the footage is not recent and relates to an incident that took place in May this year. Police issued the clarification after becoming aware that the video was being widely shared online, prompting concern among residents. Man arrested, charged and remanded According to West Yorkshire Police, a 24-year-old man was arrested in connection with the incident. The man was subsequently charged with sexual assault and exposure before being remanded in custody. Suspended prison sentence handed down Police said the case has already been dealt with by the courts. The defendant was sentenced earlier this month to 23 months' imprisonment, suspended for 18 months. The sentence followed his conviction for sexual assault and exposure offences linked to the incident. Warning against speculation West Yorkshire Police is urging members of the public not to speculate about the case on social media. The force said the incident has already been investigated, with the offender identified, charged and sentenced through the criminal justice system. Officers issued the statement to provide reassurance and clarify that the footage currently circulating online does not relate to a recent incident. FULL statement from West Yorkshire Police A WYP spokesperson said: "We are aware of a video re-circulating on social media which appears to show a man exposing himself at a bus stop in Leeds. "We can confirm that the footage is not recent and happened in May earlier this year. "A 24-year-old man, of Asian ethnicity and Czech Republic nationality, was arrested, charged and remanded for sexual assault and exposure. "He was subsequently sentenced in court this month to 23 months imprisonment suspended for 18 months. "We would urge people not to speculate on social media." The new rules issued by the Commerce Department say that overseas data centers that serve countries such as China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are mandated to identify their end users. In addition, exports of chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil will need export licenses. Those countries, according to the US government, pose an "unacceptable risk of diversion" to unauthorized destinations. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun reacted to the new US rules, saying: "China will take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests." The new curbs come ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping later this week at the APEC summit in Shenzhen. AI and chips are sure to come up during the talks between Trump and Xi.
